Q000004:
Why this is correct:
A model that systematically disadvantages a group because it learned from skewed historical decisions shows bias.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Underfitting: poor fit overall.
• Reinforcement learning: a training paradigm.
• Overfitting: memorizing training data.

Key takeaway: historical skew → biased models.
Q000005:
Why this is correct:
Very high training accuracy with much lower accuracy on new data means the model is overfitting and generalizes poorly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Must be unlabeled: no.
• Perfect fairness: unrelated.
• Underfitting: would be poor on training too.

Key takeaway: train high, test low → overfitting.
Q000007:
Why this is correct:
Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, or code. Discriminative models classify or predict from inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No training data: GenAI needs lots.
• Only tabular data: no.
• Synonymous: no.

Key takeaway: generate vs. discriminate.
Q000008:
Why this is correct:
A system that breaks goals into steps and acts autonomously with tools is agentic AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Classification model: predicts labels.
• Batch pipeline: scheduled processing.
• Relational database: storage.

Key takeaway: autonomous multi-step action → agentic AI.
Q000012:
Why this is correct:
Exact, deterministic calculations like interest accrual should use standard software, not probabilistic AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DL approximation: introduces error.
• FM generating figures: unreliable.
• Clustering: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: deterministic rules → traditional software, not AI.
Q000065:
Why this is correct:
RAG with Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock retrieves current internal documentation at query time, grounding answers without retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tune on every change: slow and costly.
• Continuous pretraining: heavy.
• Higher temperature: more random.

Key takeaway: answer from changing documents → RAG.
Q000109:
Why this is correct:
Overly strict filters can block legitimate requests, hurting usability. Safety settings must balance protection with user experience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No effect on UX: false.
• Only training: Guardrails apply at inference.
• Automatically resolved: requires tuning.

Key takeaway: safety vs. usability tradeoff.
Q000115:
Why this is correct:
Publishing full details of a fraud model could help attackers evade it. Transparency can conflict with safety and security.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No security effect: false.
• Regulators never require transparency: false.
• Always aligned: false.

Key takeaway: transparency must be balanced with security.
Q000119:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Clarify feature attribution (SHAP) shows which features most influenced a prediction.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Trusted Advisor: best practices.
• Logs Insights: logs.

Key takeaway: why a prediction → Clarify feature attribution.
Q000121:
Why this is correct:
The company may accept somewhat lower accuracy from an interpretable model to meet explainability requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No tradeoff: there is one.
• Rules only for rules-based: no.
• Unrelated: they're related.

Key takeaway: interpretability vs. accuracy tradeoff.
Q000125:

Macie scans S3 data for PII before it's used to fine-tune a model.

Why the other options are wrong:

Q000141:
Why this is correct:
Poor data quality (errors, gaps, stale records) directly degrades model performance regardless of algorithm choice.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Architecture matters more: data often dominates.
• Size beats quality: false.

Q000143:

ISO/IEC 42001 is the international standard for AI management systems, suited to aligning an AI program with governance best practices.

ISO/IEC 23053 provides a framework for describing AI systems that use machine learning, including components and functions.

Why the other options are wrong:

Q000145:
Why this is correct:
Unstructured data such as documents and images usually needs extra processing (extraction, labeling, indexing) before AI can use it.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Unstructured unusable: false.
• AI auto-structures: not automatically.

Q000146:
Why this is correct:
An AI agent can handle complex, multi-step tasks and take actions, while a scripted bot only matches keywords. Agents need more governance and cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: no.
• Always cheaper: no.
• Bot executes refunds: no.

Key takeaway: agents add capability and risk.
Q000148:
Why this is correct:
Without ongoing monitoring, the team may miss performance degradation from drift as conditions change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Monitoring only at first: false.
• Removing monitoring helps: false.
• Performance never changes: false.

Key takeaway: production models need continuous monitoring.
Q000150:
Why this is correct:
Few-shot prompting shows examples of the desired tagline style, guiding consistent outputs without training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tuning: heavier.
• RAG: retrieval of facts.
• Zero-shot: no examples.

Key takeaway: consistent style quickly → few-shot prompting.
Q000151:
Why this is correct:
When a document exceeds the context window, split it into chunks, summarize each, then combine the summaries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More examples: uses more tokens.
• Ignore the error: fails.
• Switch to rules: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: long documents → chunk and summarize.
Q000152:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning on examples of the formal style adjusts the model's parameters so it consistently writes that way.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RAG: supplies facts, not style.
• Single instruction: may not be consistent.
• Larger context: no style change.

Key takeaway: consistent specialized style → fine-tuning.
Q000153:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning needs more upfront investment in data and training. RAG is faster to start and stays current with changing data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RAG always less accurate: no.
• Fine-tuning faster and cheaper: usually not.
• No maintenance: false.

Key takeaway: fine-tuning = upfront cost; RAG = flexibility.
Q000154:
Why this is correct:
Clear instructions, relevant context, and explicit constraints (such as answering only from provided context) reduce hallucinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multiple questions: confusion.
• Longest response: more error.
• Vague prompts: more hallucination.

Key takeaway: clear, grounded prompts reduce errors.
Q000155:
Why this is correct:
Providing an explicit example of the desired format (few-shot) helps the model follow the bullet structure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Smaller context: no.
• Rule-based: unnecessary.
• Repeat same prompt: likely same result.

Key takeaway: show the format you want.
Q000156:
Why this is correct:
Weigh the higher cost of a larger context window against actual needs. Use it only where tasks require long inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always smaller: may not fit tasks.
• Always larger: wasteful.
• No cost effect: false.

Key takeaway: choose context size by need and cost.
Q000158:
Why this is correct:
With no in-house data science team and a need for speed, licensing a pre-built solution through AWS Marketplace is fastest.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Exclusive 10-year contract: lock-in.
• Build from scratch: slow.

Q000159:

Moving a vendor PoC to production requires planning for data portability, system integration, staff skills, and support to avoid lock-in and gaps.

Why the other options are wrong:

• Rebuild without reason: wasteful.
• Terminate on launch day: risky.

Q000161:

Q000162:

Q000164:
